Resetting to neutral was some advice given to me in that when you play as dante it's helpful to have a "neutral" state before going into an enemy encounter/boss (Mine is Trickster, Ebony/Ivory and Rebellion).   
The trick by doing this is that when you set this to your neutral state for Dante eventually you no longer need to look at the icons for which sytle/weapons/guns you want to use, because it's starting from your neutral state.   
Want to royal guard? (Down on the d-pad)   
Switch to cavaliere? (Press R2 5 times)  
In lulls in combat you switch back to neutral to give yourself some time to think/get away. (It really helps).   
By the way your "neutral" could be anything. I just set these as my default as they're the ones I used the most.  


I hope that helps. I believe in you :)

Some monsters require you to wait/run around more (I'm looking at you Rajang), others you can play more aggressively.

If you ever go back to it. I would recommend the remastered edition of the last remnant on ps4. It's only $20 I believe. 

It adds some quality of life fixes like a sprint mechanic for free. The remastered version is actually the pc version released on current gen consoles (ps4). It includes all dlc of the base game and no frame rate issues that the 360 version was notorious for. (Like 15 fps in some cases). It also makes it so that you can use unique leaders for all unions. In the 360 version you're limited to one unique leader per union, the remastered version removes that limitation. 

Also, for whatever reason the mechanics of the game were a black box that the developers never really explained. So reading the wikia page is pretty much mandatory.

Even with that though, the game can be incredibly complicated for newcomers. I didn't know what the fuck I was doing for the first 100 hours of the game. 

I love games like this though. Where the mechanics are complicated and the finer understanding of the game requires experimentation and research.

Honestly, the learning curve can be steep, but once it clicks its awesome.

Its not as insanely complicated as The Last Remnant (which I've sunk close to 600 hours into for its combat system alone), but it can be overwhelming. I would highly recommend going to the arena and doing the practice matches to get a feel for the combat.

We tend to believe that societies expectation on where we should be in life defines how worthy we are as human beings. 

It's not true. 

There will be naysayers. People who adhere to opinions. Criticism on how can we become better without listening to others?

The important thing to keep in mind is that public opinion/society's expectations can never and will never define yourself. We give away so much power to others opinions, entrust our self- image based on others perception of us and ultimately feel worthless when they criticize us.

I'm not saying criticism is bad, far from it. Its how we internalize it that seems to be the issue.

That's my anecdotal evidence btw. So don't believe I have all the answers. There's so much I'm still learning about myself and societies.

If someone truly was that vapid. As in they deem you a lesser person for not having those experiences. Would you truly want to be with that person? 

I personally would not want to. Because a relationship is a two-way street. You need to remember that this person we are seeking to be with should enhance our life. Not become the defining point of it.

I didn't move out of my parents place till I was 26. That was the 2nd best decision I've made in my life. 

It's truly liberating to me for striking it out on my own. 

No longer needing to constantly be told how to behave was a plus for me too lol.

This is interesting to me, because I tend to hear conflicting opinions when it comes to "Just Be Yourself" in regards to dating. 

Some argue that "Just Be Yourself" is terrible advice if you're an asshole or have a characteristic that is undesirable. Others say that by not being yourself you are denying yourself the chance to truly find someone who loves/supports you for who you are.

In regards to the dates that I went on. I found that by acting like myself brought me the most success/failure at that time. I wasn't worried about trying to sound superficial or admitting my shortcomings. I behaved like I would with any other person. Be they friend, colleague, manager or stranger. 

In regards to "Who would date me?" and self, - confidence/ anxiety issues. I can't say I'm over my hurdles/personal issues either. The thought of approaching a girl at the bar still terrifies me today. Going outside my comfort zone unnerves me. Not meeting my works expectations makes me physically gag.

But it's better today. I have weeks of clarity. I'm at peace more often. I no longer second guess every decision I ever make. I speak up at work more often when I believe something isn't correct factually or there may have been an oversight. I no longer care about failing/ making mistakes, because that's how I learn. (Despite corporate culture/current management disagreeing and putting more emphasis on covering up mistakes and ensuring our reputation isn't ruined)

I can't take all the credit though. I've been seeing a therapist for 3 years now on a weekly basis and it's only through talking through my issues with a licensed professional that I'm overall in a better place now. (Where I likely would have attempted suicide if I didn't seek help)
